1212.title: seva as vocation
1212.hook: a great ascetic is sent to a market stall to learn dharma
1212.howItsDone: Hindu teachers sometimes retell the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali from the Mahabharata to show that honest work in an ordinary trade can itself be a way of dharma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation at Yudhishthira's great sacrifice: the guest honored first took the job of washing feet.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION.` · `THE JOB AT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: A man stands in the forest so still, for so long, that a pair of birds builds a nest in his matted hair. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. His name is Jajali, an ascetic. The birds lay their eggs. The eggs hatch. He stays still until the chicks grow wings, fly off, and stop coming back. Then a thought arrives, and it's a proud one: who in the world is my equal in dharma? An unseen voice answers. Not you, Jajali. There's a merchant in Varanasi named Tuladhara, and you are not his equal.
screen: `BIRDS NEST IN HIS HAIR.` → `WHO IS MY EQUAL?` → `A MERCHANT IN VARANASI.`

segments.voice: So Jajali goes to Varanasi and finds him, a trader selling goods in the market. Before Jajali can say a word, Tuladhara greets him and tells him his own story: the stillness, the birds, the proud thought, the voice. Jajali asks the obvious question. You sell things for a living. How do you know any of this? Tuladhara's answer, in paraphrase, is the teaching. He knows the ancient dharma, he says, and he names it plainly: friendship toward all beings, and a way of living that harms them as little as it can. He earns his bread by trade, and keeps it honest. He doesn't cheat on the weight. He doesn't flatter or run anyone down to make a sale. He holds the same even scale for everyone who comes to his counter. Even his name fits. In Sanskrit, a tula is a balance, and Tuladhara can be heard as the one who holds the scales. In this story, the scale on the counter and the evenness in his mind are one practice. Now notice who's teaching whom. The great ascetic walks all the way to a market to learn from a man who weighs things for a living. The Mahabharata doesn't tell Jajali to open a shop, or call his years in the forest a waste. It says dharma was already sitting at that counter, in an honest weight handed to a customer Tuladhara might never see again. That's one face of seva as vocation: not service added on top of a job, but the way the job itself gets done.
screen: `TULADHARA TELLS JAJALI HIS OWN STORY.` · `FRIENDSHIP TOWARD ALL BEINGS.` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SCALES.` · `DHARMA AT THE SHOP COUNTER.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palm up on your knees, like the two pans of a balance, and bring to mind one exchange waiting for you: a sale, a report, a favor, a reply. Notice where you'd be tempted to tip it a little, a corner cut, a bit of flattery, then let both hands rest evenly again and breathe there. If you pray, you can offer that exchange to God as it is.
Seva as vocation. Service done through the work itself, the way Tuladhara served everyone who trusted his scales.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. A scale held level serves every buyer who trusts it, whether or not anyone notices. See you tomorrow.

1213.title: seva as vocation
1213.hook: the Gita's renouncer who never quits the job
1213.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1213.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of karma yoga turn to the opening of the Gita's sixth chapter to explain that renunciation can be practiced inwardly, by letting go of the fruit of action while continuing to work.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation at a market stall: Tuladhara held the same even scale for everyone, and taught an ascetic with birds in his hair.
screen: `TULADHARA'S LEVEL SCALE.`

segments.voice: Hand in the badge, close the laptop, move somewhere quiet, and live on rice and silence. That's the modern daydream of leaving. Hindu tradition has a real version of it. The sannyasi, the renouncer, gives up home, possessions and the household fire, and walks out of ordinary life on purpose. It's an honored path. And the Bhagavad Gita, at the opening of its sixth chapter, redraws the picture of who counts as a renouncer. Its new picture includes people who never leave their jobs.
screen: `QUIT EVERYTHING?` → `THE SANNYASI, THE RENOUNCER.` → `THE GITA REDRAWS THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The one who does the work that ought to be done, without leaning on its fruit, is a renouncer, and a yogi. Not the one who has merely put out the fire. Not the one who has merely stopped acting. Take it in pieces. The work that ought to be done: in Sanskrit, karyam karma. Not any work at all, and not only work that feels holy. The work that's actually yours to do, today. Without leaning on its fruit: the word is anashritah, not taking shelter in, not propping yourself up on. The fruit is the result: the praise, the raise, the thank-you. The verse doesn't say results don't matter. It says don't lean your whole weight on them. And the fire: commentators read it as the household's sacred fires, which a renouncer no longer tends. The outward sign isn't the thing itself. Putting out the fire doesn't make you free; letting go inwardly does. The next verse makes it plain. What people call renunciation, Krishna says, know that to be yoga, and no one becomes a yogi without letting go of their scheming. Yesterday a merchant held his scale level in a crowded market. Today the Gita says the deepest letting go can happen at that same counter, in the same shift, in the same inbox. Hindu tradition still honors those who take the robe. Read this way, the Gita leaves room for a nurse, a farmer or a clerk to renounce too, without leaving the work.
screen: `THE WORK THAT OUGHT TO BE DONE.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.` · `PUTTING OUT THE FIRE ISN'T THE THING.` · `A RENOUNCER WHO KEEPS WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you and notice the fruit you're leaning on, the reply, the approval, the result, and where that leaning lives in the body, maybe the shoulders, maybe the jaw. On each out-breath, shift your weight back onto your own two feet: the work is still there and you still care how it goes, you're just not hanging on it. If you pray, you can offer the result to God and keep the work.
Seva as vocation. In the Gita's sixth chapter, the renouncer is the one who does the work that's theirs, without leaning on its fruit.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. The renouncer isn't defined by the robe or the cabin. Back tomorrow, same hill.

screen: `DAY 1213 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BHAKTI: THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS COMPLETE.`

1214.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1214.hook: the sutras' boldest claim: love isn't the road, it's where the road goes
1214.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1214.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1214.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied in short sections with a teacher, and lines like these on love as the fruit and the Lord's fondness for humility are explained with stories of devotees.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed seva as vocation: the Gita's renouncer never quits the job, but stops leaning on the fruit.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: A road is usually a way to get somewhere. Nobody frames a photo of the on-ramp. You drive the highway to reach the beach, and once you're there, you forget the highway. Now, what if someone told you the road and the beach were the same thing? Year two opened a short book attributed to the sage Narada, the Narada Bhakti Sutras: its definition of bhakti as supreme love, and the four teachers' marks of it. For six days we read on, to the last line. And a little past where we stopped, the book makes its boldest claim.
screen: `A ROAD, OR THE PLACE IT LEADS?` → `THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS.` → `READ THROUGH TO THE END.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: bhakti, the sutras say, is greater even than karma, jnana and yoga: action, knowledge and the disciplined stilling of the mind. That sounds like a ranking, and it is. But the reason changes how it sounds. Because it is of the form of the fruit. Phala-rupa. The fruit is what the tree is for. So the sutras aren't calling the other roads worthless. They're saying love is what those roads walk toward: work done as an offering, knowing that clears the mind, a mind held still, all finding their point in love. Then a second reason, and a surprising one. The Lord, the sutras say, dislikes pride and is fond of humility. The Sanskrit for that humility is dainya: lowliness, the state of someone with empty hands. A person can turn good work into a trophy, or knowledge, or a long practice. In the sutras' picture, love has a hard time doing that, because it keeps looking at the beloved, not at itself. That's Narada's view, and the text says so plainly. Other Hindu teachers weigh the roads differently. Shankara's school, which we met in year two, holds that knowledge is what frees, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Both are living Hindu paths. And the sutras aren't done with the question. Tomorrow they ask, out loud, whether knowledge is the means to love.
screen: `GREATER THAN KARMA, JNANA AND YOGA.` · `PHALA-RUPA: LOVE IS THE FRUIT.` · `THE LORD LOVES HUMILITY.` · `NARADA'S VIEW, AMONG OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and notice anything you're holding up like a trophy today: something you did well, something you know, how long you've practiced. Don't scold it; set it down beside you the way you'd put down a bag, and rest with the hands open. If you pray, you can turn toward God with those open hands; if not, simply stay with what it's like to hold nothing up.
Bhakti. In the Narada Bhakti Sutras, not only a road but the fruit itself, and close to humility, dainya, the open hand.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. In this book, the road and the beach are one. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1214 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BHAKTI: THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS COMPLETE.`

1215.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1215.hook: is knowing about love the way to it? the sutras answer with a king and a meal
1215.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1215.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1215.howItsDone: Teachers of the Narada Bhakti Sutras use the king and the meal to explain that devotion is something lived, not only studied, and pair the study of the text with worship, singing and service.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: love is the fruit, not only the road, and the Lord is fond of humility, empty hands.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FRUIT.` · `EMPTY HANDS.`

segments.voice: A menu can be a beautiful thing. Photographs, careful descriptions, a paragraph about the farm the tomatoes came from. You could learn every word of it by heart, explain it to a friend, and walk out exactly as hungry as you came in. That small, familiar gap, between knowing about something and having it, is where the Narada Bhakti Sutras go next. If love is above the other roads, how do you get it? Isn't knowledge the way in?
screen: `READING THE MENU.` → `STILL HUNGRY.` → `ISN'T KNOWLEDGE THE WAY IN?`

segments.voice: The sutras answer the way they did on the marks of love in year two: they let several voices speak. Some say, the text reports, that knowledge alone is the means to bhakti: you have to know who the Lord is before you can love him. Others say knowledge and love depend on each other, like two cards propped into a little tent. Then a third voice, the sons of Brahma, whom commentators take to be the ever-young sages of the Puranas. They say bhakti is its own fruit, not produced by something else. Here the sutras side with them, and give their evidence: the case of a king, a house, and a meal. Knowing about a king doesn't make the king pleased with you. Knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger. You can know the palace floor plan and never be welcomed in. So, the sutras conclude, those who long for freedom should take up love itself. Notice what they don't say. Not that knowledge is bad, or that you should stop learning. Narada is a sage who knew a great deal. In the Chandogya Upanishad, which we read in year two, he comes to his teacher with a whole library in his head and admits he's still not at peace. The sutras just refuse to let knowing about stand in for the thing. The king has to be met. The meal has to be eaten.
screen: `SOME SAY: KNOWLEDGE IS THE MEANS.` · `OTHERS: EACH LEANS ON THE OTHER.` · `THE SONS OF BRAHMA: ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `KNOWING ABOUT A MEAL ISN'T EATING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you love and notice, for a few breaths, how much you know about them: their habits, their history, the facts. Then let the facts go quiet and simply be near them, the way you'd sit beside someone without needing to talk. If you pray, you can do this with God, setting aside what you know about God for a while.
Bhakti. For the sutras, its own fruit: knowing about the king doesn't please him, and knowing about the meal doesn't feed you.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. The love has to be loved. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1215 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BHAKTI: THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS COMPLETE.`

1216.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1216.hook: how does love begin? the sutras' list of means, and the one they call chief
1216.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1216.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1216.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, people gather for satsang, sitting with teachers and fellow devotees to hear and sing about God, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras' lines on the company of great souls are a familiar reason given for it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the king and the meal: knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger, and love is its own fruit.
screen: `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `ITS OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: How did you come to love the thing you love most? A kind of music, a sport, a craft, a city. Did you study your way into it? Or did someone take you along: an uncle with his records, a friend who dragged you to a game, a grandmother who let you stand at the stove? If knowledge can't produce love, how does it start? Today the sutras give a short list of means, and then name the one that matters most.
screen: `HOW DID YOU COME TO LOVE IT?` → `SOMEONE TOOK YOU ALONG.` → `THE SUTRAS' LIST OF MEANS.`

segments.voice: The teachers sing of its means, the sutras say, and list them. Letting go of the pull of sense objects, and of clinging attachment. Worship that doesn't break off. Hearing and singing the qualities of the Lord, even while living an ordinary life in the world. That last phrase matters: the means aren't only for a monastery. They happen at work, in the car, in the kitchen. Then the sutras turn. But chiefly, love comes by the grace of great souls, or by a drop of the Lord's own grace. After the list of things a person can do, the main source is something given. Then three phrases about the company of the great, mahat-sanga. It is hard to find: such people don't advertise. It is hard to fathom: from outside, it isn't easy to tell who they are. And it never fails: in the sutras' view, that company always bears fruit. How is it found? Even it, the sutras say, comes only by his grace. Then a line that holds the section together. Between him and his people, there is no difference. To be near those who love God, in this text, is already to be near God. And the section ends with a sentence said twice, like a teacher tapping the table: strive for that alone, strive for that alone. Back to your uncle with his records. In the sutras' picture, love of God can travel the same way: someone who already has it takes you along.
screen: `LET GO, WORSHIP, HEAR AND SING.` · `CHIEFLY: THE GRACE OF GREAT SOULS.` · `HARD TO FIND, NEVER FAILS.` · `NO DIFFERENCE: HIM AND HIS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a song, a chant or a name others once sang around you, at a temple, at home, in a car with the radio on, and let it play quietly inside without moving your lips. Listen the way you'd listen in a room full of people singing it together, and when the mind wanders, come back to the next line. If you pray, you can let it be a song of praise to God.
Bhakti. In the sutras it's helped along by letting go, by worship, by hearing and singing, and chiefly by the company of great souls, mahat-sanga.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. Love travels from the one who has it to the one sitting near. Same time tomorrow.

1217.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1217.hook: ripples that become an ocean, and the question asked twice: who crosses?
1217.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1217.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1217.howItsDone: Devotional teachers explain the sutras on bad company as advice to guard the mind, and pair it with the positive practice of satsang, keeping company that nourishes love of God.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the company of great souls: hard to find, hard to fathom, never failing, and no difference between the Lord and his people.
screen: `THE COMPANY OF GREAT SOULS.`

segments.voice: A ripple on a pond is nothing. A few inches high, gone in a second. Nobody builds a seawall against a ripple. But stand on a beach in a storm, and every wave there began as something small, pushed and fed and gathered until it could knock a person over. Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras turn the coin over, from the company that helps love grow to the company that does the opposite, and they reach for exactly that picture: ripples becoming an ocean.
screen: `A RIPPLE IS NOTHING.` → `A STORM WAVE BEGAN SMALL.` → `TODAY, THE OTHER COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Bad company, dussanga, is to be given up in every way, the sutras say. And they give the reason as a chain. It causes desire, then anger, then delusion, then the loss of memory, then the loss of understanding, and then the loss of everything. The Gita's second chapter has a chain much like it. Then the image: though these arise only like ripples, through company they become an ocean. A flash of desire or anger isn't a disaster in itself. A ripple is a ripple. What turns it into an ocean is company: whatever keeps feeding it, a person, a habit, a feed on a screen. Then a question, asked twice: who crosses? Who crosses over maya, the great illusion? The answer comes in short lines. The one who gives up clinging. The one who serves the great. The one who becomes free of mine. The one who seeks out a quiet place, loosens the knots that tie them to the world, and gives up worrying over getting and keeping. The one who gives up the fruit of action and goes beyond the pairs, pleasure and pain, praise and blame. The one who comes to a love that doesn't break off. And then, said twice to match the question: that one crosses, that one crosses. And a last phrase that turns it outward: and helps the worlds cross too. The one who gets across becomes a boat for others. In this picture, yesterday's great souls are the ones who crossed.
screen: `DUSSANGA: A CHAIN OF LOSSES.` · `RIPPLES BECOME AN OCEAN.` · `WHO CROSSES? WHO CROSSES?` · `AND HELPS THE WORLDS CROSS.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will rise, an irritation, a wanting, a worry; notice it the way you'd notice a ripple on water. Don't push it down and don't feed it, no replaying the argument, no adding the next thought; just watch it rise and flatten out on its own. If you pray, you can hand each ripple to God as it passes.
Bhakti. In the sutras, it's guarded from the company that turns ripples into an ocean, and it carries those who cross.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. A ripple left unfed stays a ripple. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1217 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BHAKTI: THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS COMPLETE.`

1218.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1218.hook: a taste that can't be told: the sutras on what love itself is like
1218.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1218.tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1218.howItsDone: Devotional teachers quote the sutras' image of a taste that a person who cannot speak cannot describe, to explain why bhakti is passed on through singing, stories and company rather than argument.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the ripples: through company they become an ocean, and the one who crosses helps the worlds cross too.
screen: `RIPPLES BECOME AN OCEAN.` · `WHO CROSSES?`

segments.voice: Try describing the taste of a mango to someone who has never eaten one. Sweet, you say. But not like sugar. A little like a peach, but not really. Sort of floral. Sort of like sunshine, which doesn't help at all. After a minute you give up and wish you could just hand them a slice. Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras try to say what love itself is like, and they start by admitting they can't.
screen: `DESCRIBE A MANGO.` → `YOU GIVE UP.` → `WHAT IS LOVE ITSELF LIKE?`

segments.voice: The nature of love, the sutras say, cannot be told. Anirvacaniya. Then the comparison: it's like the tasting of someone who cannot speak. The taste is completely real; it just can't get out in words. It shows itself in a vessel fit for it: not everywhere at once, not on command, but in a particular person, at a particular time. Then the sutras try anyway, with a string of qualities. It is free of the qualities that color ordinary feeling. It is free of wanting something back. It grows every moment. It doesn't break off. It is subtler than the subtle. And it is a matter of experience, not of theory. That phrase, growing every moment, is worth sitting with. The things we like can wear down with use. The song gets old. The new car stops being new. The sutras say this love does the opposite: the longer it runs, the more of it there is. And someone who has it? Having gained it, the sutras say, they see only that, hear only that, speak only of that, think only of that. Look back at the week: a merchant's even scale, the renouncer who never quit the job, love as the fruit, the king and the meal, the company of great souls, ripples and the crossing, and today, a taste that can't be told. Tomorrow, the last pages: what the sutras say about the people who have this love.
screen: `ANIRVACANIYA: IT CANNOT BE TOLD.` · `LIKE A TASTE FOR ONE WHO CAN'T SPEAK.` · `GROWING EVERY MOMENT.` · `THEY SEE ONLY THAT, HEAR ONLY THAT.`

segments.voice: Bring back a moment when you were deeply happy with someone or something you love: the light, the sound, the feeling in the chest. Each time a word tries to describe it, let the word go and go back to the taste, no commentary, no captions. If you pray, you can rest in God the same way, without words.
Bhakti. In the sutras, a love that can't be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak, and it grows every moment.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. Some things are only known by tasting. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1218 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BHAKTI: THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS COMPLETE.`
